common_name: Seiju Chinese Elm (Dwarf Corky-Bark Bonsai Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown starts in spring in fast-draining bonsai or container soil in full sun to light shade; Seiju is almost always trained as a container specimen, so repot every one to two years to manage its compact root system.

directions: Seiju is one of the most widely sold Chinese elm cultivars for bonsai, prized for its naturally tiny, dark green leaves under half an inch long and for developing thick, deeply fissured corky bark while still young rather than only at great age. Its compact internodes and dense ramification let growers achieve a convincing miniature tree silhouette within a few years of training, and it backbuds reliably after hard pruning, making it forgiving for beginners learning wiring and leaf-reduction techniques. Like the straight species it tolerates heat and a wide soil pH range and resists Dutch elm disease, but because it is almost always grown in a shallow container it needs more frequent watering and repotting than a landscape elm. Keep it in full sun to light shade, water as the soil surface dries, and repot every one to two years in spring to refresh fast-draining bonsai substrate.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Hokkaido Chinese Elm (Micro-Leaf Dwarf Bonsai Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown starts in spring in fast-draining bonsai soil in full sun to light shade; Hokkaido stays extremely dwarf even untrained, so check soil moisture daily in hot weather since its fine root system in a shallow pot dries out quickly.

directions: Hokkaido is an extreme dwarf sport of Chinese elm named for the northern Japanese island where it was selected, grown almost exclusively for shohin and mame (miniature) bonsai because of its exceptionally small leaves, often under a quarter inch long, and very short internodes that create dense twiggy ramification without heavy pruning. It is naturally slower and more compact than Seiju, staying diminutive even when left untrained, which makes it a favorite for tiny accent trees and forest-style plantings where several small trunks share one pot. Like other Chinese elm selections it tolerates a wide range of soils and resists Dutch elm disease, but its fine root system dries out quickly in shallow bonsai containers. Repot every one to two years in spring using a fast-draining bonsai mix, and prune new shoots back to one or two leaves to keep the miniature scale.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Yatsubusa Chinese Elm (Compact Fine-Twig Bonsai Elm)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown starts in spring in fast-draining bonsai or grow-box soil in full sun to light shade; Yatsubusa thickens trunks readily in a grow box before being moved to a shallow bonsai container for final styling.

directions: Yatsubusa, Japanese for roughly 'many dwarf branches,' is a compact Chinese elm selection grown for bonsai that produces noticeably shorter internodes and smaller leaves than the straight species, giving trained specimens a naturally twiggy, fine-textured canopy. It sits between Seiju and Hokkaido in ultimate scale, vigorous enough to develop trunk thickness relatively quickly in a grow box yet compact enough to finish as a believable miniature once moved to a shallow bonsai container. As with other Chinese elm cultivars it backbuds readily after defoliation or hard pruning, tolerates heat and poor soil, and resists Dutch elm disease. Grow it in full sun to light shade, keep the fast-draining bonsai substrate evenly moist through the growing season, and repot every one to two years in spring before buds break.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow it in a container as a houseplant in colder climates; Green Island stays a compact rounded mound instead of developing the invasive surface roots and towering canopy of seed-grown Ficus microcarpa.

directions: Green Island is a naturally dwarf, compact-branching selection of Ficus microcarpa that stays a dense rounded mound just a few feet tall and wide instead of growing into the towering banyan-like shade tree the species is known for, making it a popular foundation, hedge, or large container plant across South Florida and other frost-free landscapes. Its small, thick, glossy, rounded leaves crowd tightly along the stems and tolerate heavy shearing, so it is often kept as a clipped hedge or formal specimen, and its restrained, non-invasive root system makes it safer to plant near walkways and foundations than seed-grown Ficus microcarpa. In cooler climates it also performs well as a container or indoor foliage plant, tolerating lower light than many other ficus though it still drops leaves if moved abruptly or chilled. Provide bright light, consistent moisture, and protection below the high 30s Fahrenheit, and prune anytime to maintain shape since it buds back reliably from old wood.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Ficus microcarpa (Indian Laurel)

planting.note: Pot up nursery-trained specimens any time indoors in fast-draining bonsai or houseplant mix in bright indirect light; grown strictly as a container/bonsai subject, it lacks the incidental cold tolerance mature landscape Ficus microcarpa develop outdoors.

directions: Tigerbark is a bonsai-trade selection of Ficus microcarpa named for its rough, deeply furrowed, mottled gray-brown bark that develops an aged, textured look far sooner than the smoother bark of seedling-grown Indian laurel fig. Its small, glossy, pointed leaves and naturally twiggy branching make it a popular choice for growers who want a banyan-style bonsai with dramatic surface roots and trunk character without waiting decades, and it tolerates the same aggressive pruning, wiring, and defoliation techniques used on other Ficus microcarpa bonsai. Grow it indoors year-round in bright indirect light in frost-prone climates, since it drops leaves readily after a move or a chill and has none of the cold tolerance mature landscape-grown Ficus microcarpa can develop outdoors. Let the top inch of fast-draining bonsai mix dry between waterings and repot every one to two years to refresh the soil and encourage further trunk and root character.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension -- Ficus microcarpa (Indian Laurel)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in light shade to morning sun in spring or fall; afternoon shade helps protect the variegated leaf margins from scorching in hot climates.

directions: Variegata is an older Japanese zelkova selection with narrow, irregular white to cream margins around each serrated leaf, giving the canopy a lighter, more textured look than the solid green species from a distance. It shares the same graceful, multi-trunked, vase-shaped habit and resistance to Dutch elm disease as the straight species but grows more slowly and stays noticeably smaller at maturity, making it better suited to a specimen or accent role than a full-scale street tree. The variegated foliage scorches in hot, dry, full-sun exposure, so afternoon shade helps preserve leaf color through summer, and any solid-green reversion shoots should be pruned out promptly since they grow more vigorously than the variegated wood. Fall color still shifts to the bronze and orange tones typical of the species, and established trees need only routine watering beyond their first couple of seasons.

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown starts in spring in fast-draining bonsai or grow-box soil in full sun to light shade; Yatsubusa is grown specifically for bonsai and rarely reaches landscape scale.

directions: Yatsubusa is a dwarf, densely twiggy sport of Japanese zelkova selected specifically for bonsai, with much shorter internodes and smaller leaves than the species so that even young trained specimens develop the fine ramification and broom-style silhouette prized in classic zelkova bonsai. It backbuds reliably after defoliation, tolerates the same clay and urban soils as full-size zelkova, and keeps the species' strong resistance to Dutch elm disease, but its slower, more compact growth makes it far better suited to container culture than to landscape use. Give it full sun to light shade, water as the surface of the fast-draining bonsai substrate dries, and repot every one to two years in spring before buds break. Fall color still turns the bronze-orange typical of the species, just on a much smaller stage.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring or fall; Mohave was bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for strong resistance to fire blight, scab, and other diseases that trouble older pyracantha selections.

directions: Mohave is a vigorous, upright hybrid firethorn bred at the U.S. National Arboretum specifically for resistance to fire blight, scab, and the other diseases that plagued older Pyracantha coccinea selections, while still delivering the same dense fall-into-winter show of orange-red berries that covers the plant so heavily it can hide the evergreen foliage. It grows quickly into a large, thorny, informal shrub well suited to espalier against a wall, a barrier hedge, or a freestanding specimen, and like other pyracantha it flowers in white clusters in spring that draw pollinators before the berries color up. Because Mohave grows larger and more vigorously than compact cultivars, give it plenty of room and prune right after the spring bloom if size control is needed, since shearing later removes the berry-bearing wood. Full sun keeps fruiting heaviest; plants in shade bloom and fruit far less.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring or fall; Teton's narrow, columnar habit fits tighter spaces than spreading pyracantha cultivars.

directions: Teton is an upright, narrow-growing firethorn selection bred at the U.S. National Arboretum for scab resistance and a distinctly columnar habit that fits narrower spaces than spreading pyracantha cultivars, reaching considerably taller than it is wide at maturity. It produces the same abundant clusters of small white spring flowers as other pyracantha, followed by a heavy fall display of yellow-orange berries that persist into winter and draw robins, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. Its tight, upright growth makes Teton a good choice for a narrow screen, tall informal hedge, or espalier against a wall where a wide-spreading cultivar would not fit, though its stiff thorny branches still call for care when pruning or working nearby. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil for the heaviest berry set, and prune right after bloom if shaping is needed so next season's fruiting wood is not removed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension -- Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun in spring; Formosa firethorn is less cold-hardy than Pyracantha coccinea but has smaller leaves and berries that make some of its selections popular for clipped hedges, espalier, and bonsai.

directions: Formosa firethorn is a Taiwan-native pyracantha species distinguished from the more commonly planted Pyracantha coccinea by its smaller, narrower leaves, smaller red berries, and lower cold hardiness, thriving in the warmer parts of the Gulf South, coastal California, and other mild-winter climates where it holds its evergreen foliage through winter. It produces the same dense clusters of small white spring flowers followed by a heavy berry set that ripens through fall, and its fine-textured, densely thorny branching takes shearing well, making it a favorite for clipped hedges, espalier, and screening in warm climates. Because of its smaller leaf and berry scale, several Formosa firethorn selections are also grown as bonsai and trained topiary. It tolerates heat, salt spray, and poor soil once established but should be sited away from foot traffic given its stiff, sharp thorns.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
